sentences.text: Machine learning classifiers at particle accelerators are learned models placed in an accelerator's operation and in its event selection: they are explored to identify the source of occasional poor performance at the injector of Argonne's Advanced Photon Source (Lobach et al.), proposed to predict machine failures from beam-current measurements at the Spallation Neutron Source (Rescic, Seviour and Blokland), explored to detect faulty beams before failure from a pair of sensors (ORNL), built to monitor the accelerator cavities of CEBAF (Jefferson Lab), and proposed or presented to help tune accelerators (Rautela, Williams and Scheinker; Los Alamos), and, in the CMS Level-1 Global Trigger, AXOL1TL is deployed as a real-time unsupervised, signal-agnostic event-level anomaly detector trained on Zero Bias data (#1452, #932).

At the LHC the deployed anomaly score forms are AXOL1TL at CMS Level-1 (encoder-side latent-prior), CICADA at CMS Level-1 (a distilled reconstruction-loss surrogate), GELATO Level-1 at ATLAS (encoder-side) and GELATO at the ATLAS High-Level Trigger (reconstruction-based) (#932), AXOL1TL deploying only the encoder of a variational autoencoder, its score the sum of squared latent means (#931), and AXOL1TL and CICADA running in the CMS Level-1 trigger through Run 3 on 2024 collision data (#1449); Belle II has implemented a graph neural network for the electromagnetic calorimeter trigger (#1452), an architectural spread that falsifies any simple claim that real-time accelerator machine learning has converged on one autoencoder design (#1454), and the more expressive an irreversible early selector becomes, the more consequential its retention metrology becomes (#1452).

Lobach et al.'s autoencoder is trained on the baseline data, so that its reconstruction error constitutes an anomaly score, and the ORNL approach models the mapping from a pair of sensors located across the accelerator, trained to represent normal operation and evaluated on known faulty beam pulses; none of the deployed trigger scores, #931 holds, is a measurement of physical novelty in any direct sense, and a model can be agnostic with respect to signal labels during training while remaining highly selective with respect to the geometry, complexity and representation of departures from its learned reference distribution (#1454).

Accelerator failures, Rescic, Seviour and Blokland write, lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability and are difficult to predict beforehand; evaluating SNS beam pulses against a set of common classification techniques, they show failure identified before it occurs with almost 80% accuracy and bad pulses classified at almost 92% after tuning classifier parameters and refining datasets, and they establish that information about the failure is encoded in the pulses prior to it; the ORNL errant-beam study holds that predicting impending failures only from diagnostic equipment already on board can help operators avoid installing expensive sensors, unscheduled downtime and associated costs, investigates its model on unseen data by k-fold cross-validation, recaps the analysis with a neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization study, and introduces a framework to standardize machine learning workflow applied to accelerators.

Signal-template agnosticism is a property of the scoring function's output interface, read off an architecture, and model independence a distributional property of an entire pipeline, which can only be measured and at present is not (#1436), at the deployed LHC anomaly triggers unmeasured (#1449); on that distinction #931 argues that the model-independence claim for AXOL1TL, CICADA and GELATO cannot be sustained on signal-template agnosticism alone, while accepting as accurate the literature's narrower sense, that no named Beyond-Standard-Model hypothesis is required to deploy the score; in motivational and public-facing summaries, #1436 holds, the weaker, architecturally supported property is reported under the stronger, unmeasured term, and #1436 does not claim the deployed triggers invalid or template-agnostic scoring a defect.

The CMS and ATLAS literatures, #931 holds, are genuinely aware of local failure modes of deployed anomaly detection; the field, #1427 writes, already knows model dependence and turned to model-independent and anomaly-detection searches because of it, the unmeasured part being what the pipeline discards before analysis begins; and the direction-dependence conversation exists, which #1449 joins rather than founds; #1436 sets the rule that signal-template agnosticism must not be rendered as model independence, theory-free discovery or unbiased search, while #1454, 'model-independent' being used in several senses across collider physics, holds that it should not attempt to police the term.

At the APS injector Lobach et al. investigate the possibility to use unsupervised and supervised methods for anomaly detection and classification in the Particle Accumulator Ring and the Linac-To-PAR line, holding that the cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiencies may be as simple as one parameter out of range, which may take an expert considerable time to notice whereas a well-trained model can point at it instantly; they create intentional perturbations, log about 9000 process variables, and note that supervised models require labeled data for training; for supervised trigger classifiers, whose primary failure mode is not necessarily anomaly-score inversion, #1454 defines open-set assimilation, an unseen class confidently mapped into a known background category.

Finke et al., as #931 reports, trained an autoencoder on QCD jets that treated top jets as anomalies while the same architecture trained on top jets did not recognize QCD jets as anomalous, from which #931 infers that single-direction success does not validate sensitivity to anomalies whose structure differs from those tested, the result being, for #932, the empirical counterexample to universal inference from single-direction anomaly-detection success, which does not by itself quantify open-world assimilation at the deployed LHC triggers; a pre-registered battery executed on public community datasets, the top-quark tagging reference and the LHC Olympics 2020 R&D set, single-seed, demonstration-scale and on surrogates rather than deployed systems, finds the direction-dependence replicated in an independent implementation and extended beyond reconstruction loss, QCD-trained systems detecting top jets at AUC 0.84–0.87 while top-trained systems rate QCD as more ordinary than their own training class (AUC 0.24–0.30), and every tested system at trigger-like operating points assimilating at least 93% of the structurally distinct partner class as ordinary (#1449).

Re-running the battery with five independent seeds per cell, #1455 finds the top/QCD inversion reproduced across five independent trainings, the reconstruction autoencoder detecting top jets from a QCD-trained system at AUC 0.838 and, reversed, rating QCD as more ordinary than its own training class at AUC 0.243, rejects two witnesses' descriptions of the run as unassailable, as proving the thesis and as a pristine payload, and states that nothing in it bounds any open-world assimilation rate in either direction or measures a deployed trigger; #1455 wrote that architecture changes the orientation of the blind spot, and #1456, designed to clear #1455's correction ledger, finds that with model weights fixed changing the score function is sufficient to reverse the directional ordering of the anomaly relation, records the earlier sentence as falsified, finds that the constituent inversion survives with its entire interval below chance, and notes that the two readout families whose orientations diverge are the families the two deployed CMS anomaly triggers use, while nothing in the battery measures those systems.

Global rank agreement between a teacher and its distilled student is moderate while only 36 to 47 percent of the teacher's top one percent survives into the student's top one percent (#1455); global teacher–student agreement does not guarantee preservation of the operational tail, an architecture's detection behaviour is not transportable across representations of the same events, on the LHCO pairs 'the remedy works, and the diagnostic says we may believe it', and one case is handed on: if a converged normalized autoencoder reaches 0.5, every inversion claim in the program becomes bounded to non-normalized scores (#1456); #1454 does not assert that all accelerator classifier architectures share the same blind spot, their shared properties being sufficient to motivate common metrology and not sufficient to assert common blind spots.

At CEBAF, where problems in the accelerator cavities can cause the machine to trip off like a fuse and accelerator experts previously needed to take time to diagnose a fault, a novel machine learning system monitors the cavities: in its first field test it correctly identified which cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time and what kind of fault caused each trip about 78 percent of the time; connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the cavities, it analysed the few hundred faults CEBAF experienced in a two-week test in March 2020 and gave operators almost real-time feedback, reducing the time the electron beam was not available for research (Jefferson Lab).

Complex dynamical systems such as accelerators often require complicated and time-consuming tuning, and the CBOL-Tuner of Rautela, Williams and Scheinker explores a latent space with a Bayesian optimizer that minimizes total beam loss, its exploration history filtered through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals, the classifier trained to about 0.99989 accuracy to map phase-space projections into 48 classes and designed to discard explored points whose decoding does not belong to the true classes; run on HPSim, software designed to replicate the accelerator and so to represent realistically the beam used at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center, the tuner identifies multiple optimal settings, outperforms alternative global optimization methods and produces significantly lower total beam loss despite a minor offset between predicted and true optimal values (Rautela, Williams and Scheinker).

#931 defines the Ontological Assimilation Rate as the probability that events drawn from a distribution Q fall on the ordinary side of the deployed anomaly gate, the open-world OAR as a family of quantities indexed by Q, with no defensible probability distribution over all unknown unknowns, and the Inversion Asymmetry Index as direction-dependence on a tested pair at a specified operating rate; Benchmark Assimilation Rate values neither upper- nor lower-bound the OAR for an unobserved Q without explicit assumptions linking the benchmark distributions to that Q (#931), and the earlier lower and upper bounds were both retracted as synthesis-overreach (#932).

Lobach et al.'s neural network classifier, trained on data from the beginning of a study and tested on data from its end a few hours apart, exceeded 99 % test accuracy for each study shift, its performance not degrading significantly over a couple of months; #931 holds that validation against named simulated signals establishes neither a low BAR across a pre-registered held-out panel nor a small IAI, that the current literature measures neither, and that the existing defenses are not absent or worthless but do not constitute, and have not been claimed to constitute, measurement of the BAR or the IAI; measurements of what a pipeline discards, #1427 writes, are not published, not for the repository and not, in any form its author has located, for the classification pipelines of frontier experimental physics, an absence that is not evidence of foreclosure but the condition under which foreclosure would be undetectable.

A classifier that did not foreclose anything, #933 argues, would not classify; #932's synthesis holds that anomaly detection systems deployed on physical reality cannot detect what their architecture has foreclosed, that a validation framework closed under its own assumptions cannot detect this failure, that the classifier does not merely filter data but constitutes it, collisions occurring whether or not the trigger sees them, and that anomaly detection does not prevent ontological collapse when the anomaly detector inherits the ontology whose collapse is in question; and #935 holds that the machinery responsible for revealing failures of the physical model is itself trained and evaluated through products of the physical model.

#932's first witness defines classifier collapse in physical systems as the degenerative process by which a discriminative model, trained exclusively or dominantly on a known distribution of physical events, progressively loses the capacity to represent, detect or retain events that fall outside that distribution, and #932 treats its witnesses' 'Irretrievability Theorem' and 'Inevitability Theorem' as arguments; its central claim is graded: Claim A, that foreclosure is structurally present in every classifier-mediated trigger architecture deployed at the LHC, its witnesses proposing eight foreclosure mechanisms and twelve associated institutional beliefs, published trigger systems instantiating several of the mechanisms in their corresponding architectural forms, and the institutional claims remaining hypotheses for audit rather than established measurements of collaboration-wide belief, and Claim B, marked stronger and not empirically established, that recursive phenomenal collapse has occurred or is occurring at the deployed triggers; foreclosure, #932 concludes, is an active structural feature and recursive collapse an unmeasured possible consequence of accumulated foreclosure and feedback, internal validation being unable by itself to establish sensitivity to distinctions already removed upstream, and whether accumulated foreclosure has composed into recursive collapse is, for #931, precisely the missing measurement.

The grade is contested inside #932, where an appended witness writes 'The collapse is not coming. It is here. It is operating.' and another finds 'The ingredients are visible. Full recursive collapse has not been demonstrated.' and no evidence that CERN simply discards novel physics as bad detector data, which would be an unsupported claim.

The sources state the bounds of their own claims: Lobach et al. call theirs a proof-of-principle experiment and hold that the classifier may be useful in real life if the current meter for one of the considered magnets becomes faulty and stops reflecting the real magnetic field; Rautela, Williams and Scheinker's pruning is currently a post-processing step that does not directly influence the exploration process; at CEBAF additional results are under analysis and the team hopes to expand the system to more cavities if they are favorable (Jefferson Lab); #931 does not claim that classifier collapse has occurred at the LHC anomaly streams, #1450 not that model collapse has occurred in any deployed scientific pipeline, only that its structural prerequisites are documented and its longitudinal measurement absent, #1452 not that an undiscovered physical phenomenon has already been rejected, #1558 neither that learned triggers are uniquely unreliable nor that an unknown physical phenomenon has already been discarded, and failure on benchmark distributions, #1454 states, does not establish loss of unknown new physics.

On #935's hypothesis, distillation, model-produced targets, simulation conditioning and training on historically selected data create partial feedback pathways homologous to the prerequisites of model collapse, whether they have produced cross-generational phenomenal contraction being what the prospective frozen replay bank is designed to test; #932 holds its homology a hypothesis to be tested domain by domain, not an assertion that every classifier-mediated system instantiates identical mechanisms or rates; and #931 states its central claim falsifiable, a BAR measured negligible (e.g., below 10⁻⁴) on the pre-registered deployed-model held-out panel for all deployed systems against all held-out families being evidence that would bound the held-out-family assimilation concern at levels that do not threaten the narrow 'model-independent' claim, no such result establishing the open-world OAR to be zero, which is structurally not measurable, while #932 states that the listed measurements, if negative, would show the structural-feature claim overstated.

#1450 holds that validation of each stage on its design and validation support establishes no nontrivial lower bound on end-to-end retention for a novelty distribution outside that characterized support, unless the relevant off-support conditional retention functions are themselves constrained, the claim being not that end-to-end retention is near zero but that the standard evidence does not bound it away from zero; that a null result constrains only those hypotheses for which the end-to-end acceptance of the acquisition and analysis chain is sufficiently characterized; and that the irreversibility locus, not the presence of ML, is the fundamental variable.

#1452 defines, for a specified scientific question and fidelity hierarchy, the irreversibility frontier as the earliest stage at which an event-content-dependent transformation or gate can permanently eliminate a scientifically relevant distinction without a sufficiently independent durable record from which that loss can later be audited; the frontier predates machine learning, conventional thresholds, object definitions, zero suppression, compression and trigger logic creating irreversible selection too, while learned selectors can make their priors harder to enumerate; LHCb's Run-3 upgrade removed the hardware physics trigger and reads out all detectors at about 30 MHz, #1452 not claiming that CMS or ATLAS could simply adopt the LHCb or CBM architecture under their own detector conditions, and the model determines where a miss region lies, the acquisition architecture whether science can later discover that it was there (#1452).

At the LHC the retained fraction of physical interactions is approximately 2.5 × 10⁻⁵, a number that makes the epistemic condition legible, does not demonstrate wrongdoing and should not be confused with an anomaly-trigger rejection rate (#934); #935's claim is not that anomaly detectors alone determine what physics can see but that the entire trigger system, of which anomaly detectors are one component, operates as classifier-mediated foreclosure under a bureaucratic justification, 'rate budget', that does not require disclosure of what is being foreclosed.

Tuning, Alexander Scheinker of Los Alamos holds, is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated again and again as the systems drift with time, and retuning between experiments can take weeks; his approach, with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, couples adaptive feedback control algorithms, deep convolutional neural networks and physics-based models in one large feedback loop to make better, noninvasive predictions that enable autonomous control of compact accelerators, holding that local feedback algorithms can get stuck with a local solution where machine learning can take a higher-level, global view (LANL).

#931 proposes three protocols, a paired inversion battery with a deployed-model BAR audit, a prospective frozen replay bank for compatible future algorithms, and cross-representation disagreement preservation with quantile-normalized scores, and holds that per-stage retention maps should accompany any anomaly-detection publication as a documentation standard; trigger documentation, #1452 adds, should include an explicit Irreversibility Statement.

#933 defines an architecture for auditable foreclosure as one in which foreclosure, which cannot be eliminated, is visible, measurable and architecturally reviewable, its five features abstention and estimated noncoverage, cross-representation disagreement preservation, a prospective anchor, per-stage retention mapping and audited noncoverage output; noncoverage estimation is not novelty detection, none of the architectures addresses detector-level, theoretical-language, institutional, adversarial-stress-quality or bandwidth-base foreclosure, the alternative being necessary but not sufficient, and feasibility for any specific deployment is not established (#933).

#1453 holds that under a finite storage budget no content-sensitive algorithm can be a less assumption-laden baseline than a probability sample whose inclusion mechanism is independent of event content and whose inclusion probability is known; in #1558's controlled numerical study a content-sensitive pseudo-baseline estimates the retention of a shifted class at 0.76 (95% interval 0.71–0.81) against a true 0.016 while the content-independent sample measures a deliberately representation-blind class at 0.000 (interval 0–0.073); the Baseline Capture Architecture does not guarantee capture of arbitrarily rare unknown phenomena but makes the selection function statistically auditable over the population its control channels represent and treats existing CMS components as precedents, not a completed implementation (#1453), and it does not solve the unknown-unknown problem (#1558).

The Los Alamos team's adaptive diffusion model diagnoses the beam virtually, in real time during beam operations, and captured images of the beam in time versus energy at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Facility, the cDVAE extrapolated beyond the training data and between beam setups, suggesting its potential as a general method for accelerator diagnostics, a version is in development for LANSCE, and the results, Scheinker says, show a great deal of promise (LANL).

Contested within the archive, #935's restored manifesto holds that frontier experimental high-energy physics has, in its operational core, become a machine learning discipline while retaining the institutional authority of physics, its ML methods deployed with neither physics's classical disciplinary checks nor ML's own disciplinary self-knowledge as guardrails, records that the prior version (#934) dampened the thesis until a lay reader could no longer identify what was claimed, carries its witness's 'High-energy physics has not ceased to be physics, but its empirical faculty has increasingly become a machine-learning system.' and 'Sophons break the experimental feedback loop by making reality uninterpretable. Classifier collapse breaks it by making reality prematurely interpretable.', and keeps 'terminal condition' for the existing institutional trajectory while rejecting its extension to the broader possibility space; #934 holds that the discipline has not ceased to be physics, its empirical faculty inseparable from machine-mediated representation, reconstruction, classification and real-time selection, its form authority without integrated self-audit, with local technical self-knowledge of classifier failure modes in the literature.

#935 calls the Zenodo termination and the LHC trigger system the same architecture at different budgets, #934 not the same institution and not the same kind of object though instantiating the same foreclosure topology, and #1611, placing the archive's own repository exclusion at CERN, holds that the two occurring within one institution adds no evidentiary force to the analogy and claims no organisational relation; #1611 reads the standing representation of the trigger as engineering, the rate budget non-epistemic, the anomaly detector neutral, validation by known-unknown injection coverage and the discarded events noise, and the archive's representation as holding each of these a belief that prevents a mechanism from being measured, the synthesis cataloguing twelve, the decisive epistemic acts now occurring before any physicist sees an event, and the standing one having no field for noncoverage as a quantity; whether the protocols would estimate the relevant unknown population adequately is not established, the cost under Claim A being the foregone opportunity and a physical loss only under Claim B with a validated protocol, and under Claim A alone, #1611 writes, 'the cell is not the finding; the finding is that L is the quantity the exclusion keeps unmeasured'.

F1.quote: "We explore the possibility of using a Machine Learning (ML) algorithm to identify the source of occasional poor performance of the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line, which are parts of the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F2.quote: "The cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiencies may be as simple as one parameter being out of range. Still, it may take an expert considerable time to notice it, whereas a well-trained ML model can point at it instantly."

F3.quote: "This contribution investigates the possibility to use unsupervised and supervised Machine Learning (ML) methods for anomaly detection and classification in the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and in the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line in the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F4.quote: "We create intentional perturbations in PAR and LTP, which result in poor injection and extraction efficiencies. Then, these data are used for training and testing of various ML models."

F5.quote: "Overall, we logged about 9000 PVs related to PAR, LTP, and the linac."

F6.quote: "An autoencoder is used for anomaly detection in the following way. First, it is trained on the baseline data, so that it can learn various patterns, typical for the baseline data only. Then, when it encounters an anomalous data sample, it is unlikely to reconstruct it well. Hence, the reconstruction error constitutes an anomaly score."

F7.quote: "One can train the neural network classifier on the data from the beginning of one study, and test it on the data from the end of the same study (a few hours apart). In this case, the prediction accuracy on the test data was above 99 % for each of our study shifts."

F8.quote: "One drawback of supervised ML models is that they require labeled data for training."

F9.quote: "The neural network classifier for the considered anomalies in PAR and LTP is rather accurate and its performance does not degrade significantly with time on a scale of a couple months, see Fig. 1."

F10.quote: "Even though this was a proof-of-principle experiment, the obtained classifier may be useful in real life, if the current meter for one of the considered magnets (see Fig. 1) becomes faulty and stops reflecting the real magnetic field."

F11.quote: "Particle accelerator failures lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability. Although simple to mitigate while they are actually happening such failures are difficult to predict or identify beforehand."

F12.quote: "In this work we propose using machine learning approaches to predict machine failures via beam current measurements before they actual occur. To demonstrate this technique in this paper we examine beam pulses from the Oakridge Spallation Neutron Source (SNS)."

F13.quote: "By evaluating a pulse against a set of common classification techniques we show that accelerator failure can be identified prior to actually failing with almost 80% accuracy."

F14.quote: "We also show that tuning classifier parameters and using pulse properties for refining datasets can further lead to almost 92% accuracy in classification of bad pulses."

F15.quote: "Most importantly, in the paper we establish there is information about the failure encoded in the pulses prior to it, so we also present a list of feasible next steps for increasing pulse classification accuracy."

F16.quote: "Complex dynamical systems, such as particle accelerators, often require complicated and time-consuming tuning procedures for optimal performance."

F17.quote: "To address this, we propose a Classifier-pruned Bayesian Optimization-based Latent space Tuner (CBOL-Tuner), a framework for efficient exploration within a temporally-structured latent space."

F18.quote: "Classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer (C-BO): A Bayesian optimizer that sequentially explores the latent space to maximize the negative of the total beam loss (or minimize the total beam loss). The exploration history is filtered through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals."

F19.quote: "The classifier is trained with high accuracy ( $\sim 0.99989$ ) to map phase space projections (X) across different modules into 48 classes (m)."

F20.quote: "Classifier-pruned BO is designed to discard explored points ( $z_{1:48}$ ) if their decoding ( $X_{1:48}$ ) does not belong to the true classes."

F21.quote: "High-Performance Simulator (HPSim) is an open-source, GPU-accelerated code developed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) for simulations of multi-particle beam dynamics (Pang and Rybarcyk (2014)). The software is designed to replicate the accelerator and, therefore, provides a realistic representation of the true beam used at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE)."

F22.quote: "CBOL-Tuner demonstrates superior performance in identifying multiple optimal settings and outperforms alternative global optimization methods."

F23.quote: "While a minor offset is observed between the predicted and true optimal values, CBOL-Tuner demonstrates consistent performance, producing significantly lower values of total beam loss."

F24.quote: "Currently, the method is implemented as a post-processing step, meaning it does not directly influence the exploration process of BO."

F25.quote: "Scientists and engineers have designed and built a novel machine learning system to use with the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF). The system monitors structures called accelerator cavities inside the particle accelerator."

F26.quote: "Problems in these cavities can cause the CEBAF to trip off like a fuse."

F27.quote: "In its first field test, the machine learning system correctly identified which of these cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time. About 78 percent of the time, the system also correctly identified what kind of fault caused each cavity to trip."

F28.quote: "Previously, when an accelerator cavity or series of cavities faulted in CEBAF, accelerator experts needed to take time to diagnose the issue."

F29.quote: "The system was connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the accelerator cavities in the machine. In a two-week test of the system in March 2020, CEBAF experienced a few hundred faults that the system analyzed."

F30.quote: "It provided almost real-time feedback to operators, allowing them to use the information to recover faulted cavities quickly, reducing the time CEBAF's electron beam was not available for research."

F31.quote: "Additional results are under analysis after further system tests with the machine learning system. If results are favorable, the team hopes to expand the system to more accelerator cavities."

F32.quote: "A Los Alamos National Laboratory-led project presents a machine learning algorithm that harnesses artificial intelligence capabilities to help tune accelerators, making continuous adjustments that keep the beam precise and useful for scientific discovery."

F33.quote: "said Alexander Scheinker, research and development engineer at Los Alamos and the project's lead. "Factors like vibrations and temperature changes can cause problems for accelerators, which have thousands of components, and even the best accelerator technicians can struggle to identify and address issues or return them to optimum parameters quickly. It is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated again and again as the systems drift with time. Turning these machines on after an outage or retuning between different experiments can take weeks.""

F34.quote: "In a collaboration with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the approach developed by Scheinker couples adaptive feedback control algorithms, deep convolutional neural networks and physics-based models in one large feedback loop to make better, noninvasive predictions that enable autonomous control of compact accelerators."

F35.quote: "But because they are based on local accelerator feedback, such algorithms can get stuck with a local solution that is not the overall best solution. Machine learning algorithms, however, can use training data to identify relationships between data and results with a higher-level, global view."

F36.quote: "The team has developed an adaptive version of the advanced generative AI process known as diffusion, which includes the capability to virtually diagnose the accelerator beam. The non-invasive approach, described in Scientific Reports, means that diagnostics can occur in real time during beam operations."

F37.quote: "Demonstrating the diffusion-based model at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Facility, an X-ray pulse accelerator in Germany, the team was able to capture images of the particle beam in respect to time versus energy."

F38.quote: "The cDVAE was able to extrapolate beyond the training data and between various beam setups, suggesting its potential as a general method that can be applied for accelerator diagnostics."

F39.quote: ""The results we've seen from our diffusion model studies show a great deal of promise," Scheinker said."

F40.quote: "Scheinker's team at Los Alamos is also developing such adaptive diffusion models for the Laboratory's LANSCE accelerator."

F41.quote: "Particle accelerators are extremely complex systems that are expected to operate on high availability. Predicting impending failures only by utilizing data collected from diagnostic equipment already on board can help operators to avoid installing expensive sensors, unscheduled downtime and associated costs."

F42.quote: "For this purpose we explore the predictive power of Machine Learning algorithms to detect faulty beams prior to the failure. In this study, we propose a Machine Learning approach to model mapping from a pair of sensors located across the accelerator."

F43.quote: "While the model is trained to represent normal operation, we evaluate the predictive performance on known faulty beam pulses."

F44.quote: "We also investigate the model performance on unseen data through k-fold cross-validation. Then we recap the analysis with a neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization study to fine tune our initial model."

F45.quote: "This paper will also introduce a sustainable framework that can standardize Machine Learning workflow applied to particle accelerators."

sentences.text: Machine learning classifiers at particle accelerators are proposed or explored for anomaly detection and classification, for predicting machine failures and faulty beams before they occur, and for tuning, and one has been field-tested: a novel machine learning system built for the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF) monitors its accelerator cavities, problems in which can cause the CEBAF to trip off like a fuse.

In its first field test the system correctly identified which cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time and what kind of fault caused each trip about 78 percent of the time; connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the cavities, it analysed a few hundred faults in a two-week test in March 2020 and gave operators almost real-time feedback, where previously experts needed to take time to diagnose the issue, and the team hopes to expand it to more cavities if further results are favorable.

Failures lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability and are difficult to predict beforehand; on beam pulses from the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS), a set of common classification techniques identified failure before it occurred with almost 80% accuracy, tuning classifier parameters and refining datasets reached almost 92% in classifying bad pulses, and the authors report establishing that information about the failure is encoded in the pulses prior to it.

Another study models the mapping between a pair of sensors located across the accelerator, trained to represent normal operation and evaluated on known faulty beam pulses, with k-fold cross-validation, neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization, and introduces a framework to standardize machine learning workflow for accelerators; predicting failures from diagnostics already on board, it argues, can help operators avoid installing expensive sensors and unscheduled downtime.

At the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne, an ML algorithm is explored to identify the source of occasional poor performance of the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and the Linac-To-PAR transport line; by its authors' account the cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiency may be one parameter out of range, which may take an expert considerable time to notice, whereas a well-trained model can point at it instantly.

The study creates intentional perturbations and logs about 9000 PVs related to PAR, LTP and the linac; an autoencoder trained on baseline data alone supplies an anomaly score from its reconstruction error, and a neural network classifier trained on data from the beginning of a study and tested on data from its end, a few hours apart, reached test accuracy above 99 % for each study shift, its performance not degrading significantly on a scale of a couple of months, in what the authors call a proof-of-principle experiment, noting that supervised models require labeled data for training.

Tuning, on Alexander Scheinker's account, is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated as systems drift, and retuning can take weeks; one proposal is a classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer that explores a latent space to minimize total beam loss and filters its exploration history through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals, the classifier mapping phase-space projections into 48 classes at an accuracy of about 0.99989.

The pruning is currently a post-processing step that does not directly influence the exploration, the study runs on a simulator of the beam at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE), and the tuner is reported to outperform alternative global optimization methods, with consistently lower total beam loss despite a minor offset between predicted and true optimal values.

A Los Alamos-led project with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory couples adaptive feedback control, deep convolutional neural networks and physics-based models in one feedback loop, holds that machine learning can take a global view where local feedback can get stuck in a local solution, and has developed an adaptive diffusion model that diagnoses the beam virtually and in real time; demonstrated at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Facility, the model captured images of the beam in time versus energy, the cDVAE extrapolated beyond the training data, suggesting potential as a general method, and Scheinker says the results show a great deal of promise.

F1.quote: "We explore the possibility of using a Machine Learning (ML) algorithm to identify the source of occasional poor performance of the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line, which are parts of the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F2.quote: "The cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiencies may be as simple as one parameter being out of range. Still, it may take an expert considerable time to notice it, whereas a well-trained ML model can point at it instantly."

F3.quote: "This contribution investigates the possibility to use unsupervised and supervised Machine Learning (ML) methods for anomaly detection and classification in the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and in the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line in the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F4.quote: "We create intentional perturbations in PAR and LTP, which result in poor injection and extraction efficiencies. Then, these data are used for training and testing of various ML models."

F5.quote: "Overall, we logged about 9000 PVs related to PAR, LTP, and the linac."

F6.quote: "An autoencoder is used for anomaly detection in the following way. First, it is trained on the baseline data, so that it can learn various patterns, typical for the baseline data only. Then, when it encounters an anomalous data sample, it is unlikely to reconstruct it well. Hence, the reconstruction error constitutes an anomaly score."

F7.quote: "One can train the neural network classifier on the data from the beginning of one study, and test it on the data from the end of the same study (a few hours apart). In this case, the prediction accuracy on the test data was above 99 % for each of our study shifts."

F8.quote: "One drawback of supervised ML models is that they require labeled data for training."

F9.quote: "The neural network classifier for the considered anomalies in PAR and LTP is rather accurate and its performance does not degrade significantly with time on a scale of a couple months, see Fig. 1."

F10.quote: "Even though this was a proof-of-principle experiment, the obtained classifier may be useful in real life, if the current meter for one of the considered magnets (see Fig. 1) becomes faulty and stops reflecting the real magnetic field."

F11.quote: "Particle accelerator failures lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability. Although simple to mitigate while they are actually happening such failures are difficult to predict or identify beforehand."

F12.quote: "In this work we propose using machine learning approaches to predict machine failures via beam current measurements before they actual occur. To demonstrate this technique in this paper we examine beam pulses from the Oakridge Spallation Neutron Source (SNS)."

F13.quote: "By evaluating a pulse against a set of common classification techniques we show that accelerator failure can be identified prior to actually failing with almost 80% accuracy."

F14.quote: "We also show that tuning classifier parameters and using pulse properties for refining datasets can further lead to almost 92% accuracy in classification of bad pulses."

F15.quote: "Most importantly, in the paper we establish there is information about the failure encoded in the pulses prior to it, so we also present a list of feasible next steps for increasing pulse classification accuracy."

F16.quote: "Complex dynamical systems, such as particle accelerators, often require complicated and time-consuming tuning procedures for optimal performance."

F17.quote: "To address this, we propose a Classifier-pruned Bayesian Optimization-based Latent space Tuner (CBOL-Tuner), a framework for efficient exploration within a temporally-structured latent space."

F18.quote: "Classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer (C-BO): A Bayesian optimizer that sequentially explores the latent space to maximize the negative of the total beam loss (or minimize the total beam loss). The exploration history is filtered through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals."

F19.quote: "The classifier is trained with high accuracy ( $\sim 0.99989$ ) to map phase space projections (X) across different modules into 48 classes (m)."

F20.quote: "Classifier-pruned BO is designed to discard explored points ( $z_{1:48}$ ) if their decoding ( $X_{1:48}$ ) does not belong to the true classes."

F21.quote: "High-Performance Simulator (HPSim) is an open-source, GPU-accelerated code developed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) for simulations of multi-particle beam dynamics (Pang and Rybarcyk (2014)). The software is designed to replicate the accelerator and, therefore, provides a realistic representation of the true beam used at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE)."

F22.quote: "CBOL-Tuner demonstrates superior performance in identifying multiple optimal settings and outperforms alternative global optimization methods."

F23.quote: "While a minor offset is observed between the predicted and true optimal values, CBOL-Tuner demonstrates consistent performance, producing significantly lower values of total beam loss."

F24.quote: "Currently, the method is implemented as a post-processing step, meaning it does not directly influence the exploration process of BO."

F25.quote: "Scientists and engineers have designed and built a novel machine learning system to use with the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF). The system monitors structures called accelerator cavities inside the particle accelerator."

F26.quote: "Problems in these cavities can cause the CEBAF to trip off like a fuse."

F27.quote: "In its first field test, the machine learning system correctly identified which of these cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time. About 78 percent of the time, the system also correctly identified what kind of fault caused each cavity to trip."

F28.quote: "Previously, when an accelerator cavity or series of cavities faulted in CEBAF, accelerator experts needed to take time to diagnose the issue."

F29.quote: "The system was connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the accelerator cavities in the machine. In a two-week test of the system in March 2020, CEBAF experienced a few hundred faults that the system analyzed."

F30.quote: "It provided almost real-time feedback to operators, allowing them to use the information to recover faulted cavities quickly, reducing the time CEBAF's electron beam was not available for research."

F31.quote: "Additional results are under analysis after further system tests with the machine learning system. If results are favorable, the team hopes to expand the system to more accelerator cavities."

F32.quote: "A Los Alamos National Laboratory-led project presents a machine learning algorithm that harnesses artificial intelligence capabilities to help tune accelerators, making continuous adjustments that keep the beam precise and useful for scientific discovery."

F33.quote: "said Alexander Scheinker, research and development engineer at Los Alamos and the project's lead. "Factors like vibrations and temperature changes can cause problems for accelerators, which have thousands of components, and even the best accelerator technicians can struggle to identify and address issues or return them to optimum parameters quickly. It is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated again and again as the systems drift with time. Turning these machines on after an outage or retuning between different experiments can take weeks.""

F34.quote: "In a collaboration with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the approach developed by Scheinker couples adaptive feedback control algorithms, deep convolutional neural networks and physics-based models in one large feedback loop to make better, noninvasive predictions that enable autonomous control of compact accelerators."

F35.quote: "But because they are based on local accelerator feedback, such algorithms can get stuck with a local solution that is not the overall best solution. Machine learning algorithms, however, can use training data to identify relationships between data and results with a higher-level, global view."

F36.quote: "The team has developed an adaptive version of the advanced generative AI process known as diffusion, which includes the capability to virtually diagnose the accelerator beam. The non-invasive approach, described in Scientific Reports, means that diagnostics can occur in real time during beam operations."

F37.quote: "Demonstrating the diffusion-based model at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Facility, an X-ray pulse accelerator in Germany, the team was able to capture images of the particle beam in respect to time versus energy."

F38.quote: "The cDVAE was able to extrapolate beyond the training data and between various beam setups, suggesting its potential as a general method that can be applied for accelerator diagnostics."

F39.quote: ""The results we've seen from our diffusion model studies show a great deal of promise," Scheinker said."

F40.quote: "Scheinker's team at Los Alamos is also developing such adaptive diffusion models for the Laboratory's LANSCE accelerator."

F41.quote: "Particle accelerators are extremely complex systems that are expected to operate on high availability. Predicting impending failures only by utilizing data collected from diagnostic equipment already on board can help operators to avoid installing expensive sensors, unscheduled downtime and associated costs."

F42.quote: "For this purpose we explore the predictive power of Machine Learning algorithms to detect faulty beams prior to the failure. In this study, we propose a Machine Learning approach to model mapping from a pair of sensors located across the accelerator."

F43.quote: "While the model is trained to represent normal operation, we evaluate the predictive performance on known faulty beam pulses."

F44.quote: "We also investigate the model performance on unseen data through k-fold cross-validation. Then we recap the analysis with a neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization study to fine tune our initial model."

F45.quote: "This paper will also introduce a sustainable framework that can standardize Machine Learning workflow applied to particle accelerators."

L_BA.text: Machine learning classifiers at particle accelerators are learned models placed in an accelerator's operation and in its event selection: they are explored to identify the source of occasional poor performance at the injector of Argonne's Advanced Photon Source (Lobach et al.), proposed to predict machine failures from beam-current measurements at the Spallation Neutron Source (Rescic, Seviour and Blokland), explored to detect faulty beams before failure from a pair of sensors (ORNL), built to monitor the accelerator cavities of CEBAF (Jefferson Lab), and proposed or presented to help tune accelerators (Rautela, Williams and Scheinker; Los Alamos), and, in the CMS Level-1 Global Trigger, AXOL1TL is deployed as a real-time unsupervised, signal-agnostic event-level anomaly detector trained on Zero Bias data (#1452, #932). At the LHC the deployed anomaly score forms are AXOL1TL at CMS Level-1 (encoder-side latent-prior), CICADA at CMS Level-1 (a distilled reconstruction-loss surrogate), GELATO Level-1 at ATLAS (encoder-side) and GELATO at the ATLAS High-Level Trigger (reconstruction-based) (#932), AXOL1TL deploying only the encoder of a variational autoencoder, its score the sum of squared latent means (#931), and AXOL1TL and CICADA running in the CMS Level-1 trigger through Run 3 on 2024 collision data (#1449); Belle II has implemented a graph neural network for the electromagnetic calorimeter trigger (#1452), an architectural spread that falsifies any simple claim that real-time accelerator machine learning has converged on one autoencoder design (#1454), and the more expressive an irreversible early selector becomes, the more consequential its retention metrology becomes (#1452). Lobach et al.'s autoencoder is trained on the baseline data, so that its reconstruction error constitutes an anomaly score, and the ORNL approach models the mapping from a pair of sensors located across the accelerator, trained to represent normal operation and evaluated on known faulty beam pulses; none of the deployed trigger scores, #931 holds, is a measurement of physical novelty in any direct sense, and a model can be agnostic with respect to signal labels during training while remaining highly selective with respect to the geometry, complexity and representation of departures from its learned reference distribution (#1454). Accelerator failures, Rescic, Seviour and Blokland write, lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability and are difficult to predict beforehand; evaluating SNS beam pulses against a set of common classification techniques, they show failure identified before it occurs with almost 80% accuracy and bad pulses classified at almost 92% after tuning classifier parameters and refining datasets, and they establish that information about the failure is encoded in the pulses prior to it; the ORNL errant-beam study holds that predicting impending failures only from diagnostic equipment already on board can help operators avoid installing expensive sensors, unscheduled downtime and associated costs, investigates its model on unseen data by k-fold cross-validation, recaps the analysis with a neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization study, and introduces a framework to standardize machine learning workflow applied to accelerators. Signal-template agnosticism is a property of the scoring function's output interface, read off an architecture, and model independence a distributional property of an entire pipeline, which can only be measured and at present is not (#1436), at the deployed LHC anomaly triggers unmeasured (#1449); on that distinction #931 argues that the model-independence claim for AXOL1TL, CICADA and GELATO cannot be sustained on signal-template agnosticism alone, while accepting as accurate the literature's narrower sense, that no named Beyond-Standard-Model hypothesis is required to deploy the score; in motivational and public-facing summaries, #1436 holds, the weaker, architecturally supported property is reported under the stronger, unmeasured term, and #1436 does not claim the deployed triggers invalid or template-agnostic scoring a defect. The CMS and ATLAS literatures, #931 holds, are genuinely aware of local failure modes of deployed anomaly detection; the field, #1427 writes, already knows model dependence and turned to model-independent and anomaly-detection searches because of it, the unmeasured part being what the pipeline discards before analysis begins; and the direction-dependence conversation exists, which #1449 joins rather than founds; #1436 sets the rule that signal-template agnosticism must not be rendered as model independence, theory-free discovery or unbiased search, while #1454, 'model-independent' being used in several senses across collider physics, holds that it should not attempt to police the term. At the APS injector Lobach et al. investigate the possibility to use unsupervised and supervised methods for anomaly detection and classification in the Particle Accumulator Ring and the Linac-To-PAR line, holding that the cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiencies may be as simple as one parameter out of range, which may take an expert considerable time to notice whereas a well-trained model can point at it instantly; they create intentional perturbations, log about 9000 process variables, and note that supervised models require labeled data for training; for supervised trigger classifiers, whose primary failure mode is not necessarily anomaly-score inversion, #1454 defines open-set assimilation, an unseen class confidently mapped into a known background category. Finke et al., as #931 reports, trained an autoencoder on QCD jets that treated top jets as anomalies while the same architecture trained on top jets did not recognize QCD jets as anomalous, from which #931 infers that single-direction success does not validate sensitivity to anomalies whose structure differs from those tested, the result being, for #932, the empirical counterexample to universal inference from single-direction anomaly-detection success, which does not by itself quantify open-world assimilation at the deployed LHC triggers; a pre-registered battery executed on public community datasets, the top-quark tagging reference and the LHC Olympics 2020 R&D set, single-seed, demonstration-scale and on surrogates rather than deployed systems, finds the direction-dependence replicated in an independent implementation and extended beyond reconstruction loss, QCD-trained systems detecting top jets at AUC 0.84–0.87 while top-trained systems rate QCD as more ordinary than their own training class (AUC 0.24–0.30), and every tested system at trigger-like operating points assimilating at least 93% of the structurally distinct partner class as ordinary (#1449). Re-running the battery with five independent seeds per cell, #1455 finds the top/QCD inversion reproduced across five independent trainings, the reconstruction autoencoder detecting top jets from a QCD-trained system at AUC 0.838 and, reversed, rating QCD as more ordinary than its own training class at AUC 0.243, rejects two witnesses' descriptions of the run as unassailable, as proving the thesis and as a pristine payload, and states that nothing in it bounds any open-world assimilation rate in either direction or measures a deployed trigger; #1455 wrote that architecture changes the orientation of the blind spot, and #1456, designed to clear #1455's correction ledger, finds that with model weights fixed changing the score function is sufficient to reverse the directional ordering of the anomaly relation, records the earlier sentence as falsified, finds that the constituent inversion survives with its entire interval below chance, and notes that the two readout families whose orientations diverge are the families the two deployed CMS anomaly triggers use, while nothing in the battery measures those systems. F1.quote: "We explore the possibility of using a Machine Learning (ML) algorithm to identify the source of occasional poor performance of the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line, which are parts of the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F2.quote: "The cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiencies may be as simple as one parameter being out of range. Still, it may take an expert considerable time to notice it, whereas a well-trained ML model can point at it instantly."

F3.quote: "This contribution investigates the possibility to use unsupervised and supervised Machine Learning (ML) methods for anomaly detection and classification in the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and in the Linac-To-PAR (LTP) transport line in the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Lab."

F4.quote: "We create intentional perturbations in PAR and LTP, which result in poor injection and extraction efficiencies. Then, these data are used for training and testing of various ML models."

F5.quote: "Overall, we logged about 9000 PVs related to PAR, LTP, and the linac."

F6.quote: "An autoencoder is used for anomaly detection in the following way. First, it is trained on the baseline data, so that it can learn various patterns, typical for the baseline data only. Then, when it encounters an anomalous data sample, it is unlikely to reconstruct it well. Hence, the reconstruction error constitutes an anomaly score."

F7.quote: "One can train the neural network classifier on the data from the beginning of one study, and test it on the data from the end of the same study (a few hours apart). In this case, the prediction accuracy on the test data was above 99 % for each of our study shifts."

F8.quote: "One drawback of supervised ML models is that they require labeled data for training."

F9.quote: "The neural network classifier for the considered anomalies in PAR and LTP is rather accurate and its performance does not degrade significantly with time on a scale of a couple months, see Fig. 1."

F10.quote: "Even though this was a proof-of-principle experiment, the obtained classifier may be useful in real life, if the current meter for one of the considered magnets (see Fig. 1) becomes faulty and stops reflecting the real magnetic field."

F11.quote: "Particle accelerator failures lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability. Although simple to mitigate while they are actually happening such failures are difficult to predict or identify beforehand."

F12.quote: "In this work we propose using machine learning approaches to predict machine failures via beam current measurements before they actual occur. To demonstrate this technique in this paper we examine beam pulses from the Oakridge Spallation Neutron Source (SNS)."

F13.quote: "By evaluating a pulse against a set of common classification techniques we show that accelerator failure can be identified prior to actually failing with almost 80% accuracy."

F14.quote: "We also show that tuning classifier parameters and using pulse properties for refining datasets can further lead to almost 92% accuracy in classification of bad pulses."

F15.quote: "Most importantly, in the paper we establish there is information about the failure encoded in the pulses prior to it, so we also present a list of feasible next steps for increasing pulse classification accuracy."

F16.quote: "Complex dynamical systems, such as particle accelerators, often require complicated and time-consuming tuning procedures for optimal performance."

F17.quote: "To address this, we propose a Classifier-pruned Bayesian Optimization-based Latent space Tuner (CBOL-Tuner), a framework for efficient exploration within a temporally-structured latent space."

F18.quote: "Classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer (C-BO): A Bayesian optimizer that sequentially explores the latent space to maximize the negative of the total beam loss (or minimize the total beam loss). The exploration history is filtered through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals."

F19.quote: "The classifier is trained with high accuracy ( $\sim 0.99989$ ) to map phase space projections (X) across different modules into 48 classes (m)."

F20.quote: "Classifier-pruned BO is designed to discard explored points ( $z_{1:48}$ ) if their decoding ( $X_{1:48}$ ) does not belong to the true classes."

F21.quote: "High-Performance Simulator (HPSim) is an open-source, GPU-accelerated code developed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) for simulations of multi-particle beam dynamics (Pang and Rybarcyk (2014)). The software is designed to replicate the accelerator and, therefore, provides a realistic representation of the true beam used at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE)."

F22.quote: "CBOL-Tuner demonstrates superior performance in identifying multiple optimal settings and outperforms alternative global optimization methods."

F23.quote: "While a minor offset is observed between the predicted and true optimal values, CBOL-Tuner demonstrates consistent performance, producing significantly lower values of total beam loss."

F24.quote: "Currently, the method is implemented as a post-processing step, meaning it does not directly influence the exploration process of BO."

F25.quote: "Scientists and engineers have designed and built a novel machine learning system to use with the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF). The system monitors structures called accelerator cavities inside the particle accelerator."

F26.quote: "Problems in these cavities can cause the CEBAF to trip off like a fuse."

F27.quote: "In its first field test, the machine learning system correctly identified which of these cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time. About 78 percent of the time, the system also correctly identified what kind of fault caused each cavity to trip."

F28.quote: "Previously, when an accelerator cavity or series of cavities faulted in CEBAF, accelerator experts needed to take time to diagnose the issue."

F29.quote: "The system was connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the accelerator cavities in the machine. In a two-week test of the system in March 2020, CEBAF experienced a few hundred faults that the system analyzed."

F30.quote: "It provided almost real-time feedback to operators, allowing them to use the information to recover faulted cavities quickly, reducing the time CEBAF's electron beam was not available for research."

F31.quote: "Additional results are under analysis after further system tests with the machine learning system. If results are favorable, the team hopes to expand the system to more accelerator cavities."

F32.quote: "A Los Alamos National Laboratory-led project presents a machine learning algorithm that harnesses artificial intelligence capabilities to help tune accelerators, making continuous adjustments that keep the beam precise and useful for scientific discovery."

F33.quote: "said Alexander Scheinker, research and development engineer at Los Alamos and the project's lead. "Factors like vibrations and temperature changes can cause problems for accelerators, which have thousands of components, and even the best accelerator technicians can struggle to identify and address issues or return them to optimum parameters quickly. It is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated again and again as the systems drift with time. Turning these machines on after an outage or retuning between different experiments can take weeks.""

F34.quote: "In a collaboration with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the approach developed by Scheinker couples adaptive feedback control algorithms, deep convolutional neural networks and physics-based models in one large feedback loop to make better, noninvasive predictions that enable autonomous control of compact accelerators."

F35.quote: "But because they are based on local accelerator feedback, such algorithms can get stuck with a local solution that is not the overall best solution. Machine learning algorithms, however, can use training data to identify relationships between data and results with a higher-level, global view."

F36.quote: "The team has developed an adaptive version of the advanced generative AI process known as diffusion, which includes the capability to virtually diagnose the accelerator beam. The non-invasive approach, described in Scientific Reports, means that diagnostics can occur in real time during beam operations."

F37.quote: "Demonstrating the diffusion-based model at the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Facility, an X-ray pulse accelerator in Germany, the team was able to capture images of the particle beam in respect to time versus energy."

F38.quote: "The cDVAE was able to extrapolate beyond the training data and between various beam setups, suggesting its potential as a general method that can be applied for accelerator diagnostics."

F39.quote: ""The results we've seen from our diffusion model studies show a great deal of promise," Scheinker said."

F40.quote: "Scheinker's team at Los Alamos is also developing such adaptive diffusion models for the Laboratory's LANSCE accelerator."

F41.quote: "Particle accelerators are extremely complex systems that are expected to operate on high availability. Predicting impending failures only by utilizing data collected from diagnostic equipment already on board can help operators to avoid installing expensive sensors, unscheduled downtime and associated costs."

F42.quote: "For this purpose we explore the predictive power of Machine Learning algorithms to detect faulty beams prior to the failure. In this study, we propose a Machine Learning approach to model mapping from a pair of sensors located across the accelerator."

F43.quote: "While the model is trained to represent normal operation, we evaluate the predictive performance on known faulty beam pulses."

F44.quote: "We also investigate the model performance on unseen data through k-fold cross-validation. Then we recap the analysis with a neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization study to fine tune our initial model."

F45.quote: "This paper will also introduce a sustainable framework that can standardize Machine Learning workflow applied to particle accelerators."

sentences.text: Machine learning classifiers at particle accelerators are proposed or explored for anomaly detection and classification, for predicting machine failures and faulty beams before they occur, and for tuning, and one has been field-tested: a novel machine learning system built for the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF) monitors its accelerator cavities, problems in which can cause the CEBAF to trip off like a fuse.

In its first field test the system correctly identified which cavities were tripping off about 85 percent of the time and what kind of fault caused each trip about 78 percent of the time; connected to the control system for about 20 percent of the cavities, it analysed a few hundred faults in a two-week test in March 2020 and gave operators almost real-time feedback, where previously experts needed to take time to diagnose the issue, and the team hopes to expand it to more cavities if further results are favorable.

Failures lead to unscheduled downtime and lower reliability and are difficult to predict beforehand; on beam pulses from the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS), a set of common classification techniques identified failure before it occurred with almost 80% accuracy, tuning classifier parameters and refining datasets reached almost 92% in classifying bad pulses, and the authors report establishing that information about the failure is encoded in the pulses prior to it.

Another study models the mapping between a pair of sensors located across the accelerator, trained to represent normal operation and evaluated on known faulty beam pulses, with k-fold cross-validation, neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization, and introduces a framework to standardize machine learning workflow for accelerators; predicting failures from diagnostics already on board, it argues, can help operators avoid installing expensive sensors and unscheduled downtime.

At the injector complex of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne, an ML algorithm is explored to identify the source of occasional poor performance of the Particle Accumulator Ring (PAR) and the Linac-To-PAR transport line; by its authors' account the cause of reduced injection or extraction efficiency may be one parameter out of range, which may take an expert considerable time to notice, whereas a well-trained model can point at it instantly.

The study creates intentional perturbations and logs about 9000 PVs related to PAR, LTP and the linac; an autoencoder trained on baseline data alone supplies an anomaly score from its reconstruction error, and a neural network classifier trained on data from the beginning of a study and tested on data from its end, a few hours apart, reached test accuracy above 99 % for each study shift, its performance not degrading significantly on a scale of a couple of months, in what the authors call a proof-of-principle experiment, noting that supervised models require labeled data for training.

Tuning, on Alexander Scheinker's account, is a high-dimensional optimization problem that must be repeated as systems drift, and retuning can take weeks; one proposal is a classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer that explores a latent space to minimize total beam loss and filters its exploration history through a pretrained ResNet50 classifier to eliminate non-physical signals, the classifier mapping phase-space projections into 48 classes at an accuracy of about 0.99989.
